message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Freezing point (°C) |
|----------|---------------------|
| 10 kPa (≈ 0.1 atm) | **≈ –2.5 °C** |

**Why it’s lower than 0 °C**

- Water’s solid phase (ice) is *less dense* than its liquid phase.  
- When pressure is reduced, the equilibrium between ice and liquid shifts toward the phase with the larger volume (liquid).  
- Consequently, the temperature at which ice and liquid coexist (the freezing/melting point) drops below 0 °C.

**Typical values**

| Pressure | Freezing point (°C) |
|----------|---------------------|
| 1 atm (101.3 kPa) | 0.0 °C |
| 10 kPa | –2.5 °C |
| 1 kPa | –3.0 °C |
| 0.6 kPa (triple point) | 0.01 °C |

So, at 10 kPa, water will freeze at roughly **–2.5 °C**.
